module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Wieferich primes

A Wieferich prime is a prime $p$ with $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$. The only known examples are
$1093$ and $3511$. It is conjectured that there are infinitely many Wieferich primes; a heuristic
argument suggests that the number of Wieferich primes up to $x$ grows like $\log \log x$.

More generally, a prime $p$ is a Wieferich prime to base $a$ if $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$.
Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems also asks whether there are infinitely many Wieferich primes
to every base $a > 0$, and whether there is any Wieferich prime to base $47$. It is also not known
whether there is any Wieferich prime besides $1093$ and $3511$.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [Wikipedia, Wieferich prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wieferich_prime)
* [OEIS A001220](https://oeis.org/A001220)
* P. Ribenboim, *Die Welt der Primzahlen*, 2nd ed., Springer (2006), pp. 242–243.
* [PrimeGrid, Wieferich and Wall–Sun–Sun Prime Search](https://www.primegrid.com/stats_ww.php)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace WieferichPrime

/-- There are infinitely many Wieferich primes. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_isWieferichPrime : {p : ℕ | IsWieferichPrime p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Are $1093$ and $3511$ the only Wieferich primes? They are the only known ones: PrimeGrid's search,
completed in 2022, shows that any other Wieferich prime exceeds $2^{64}$. On the other hand, the
heuristic count of $\log \log x$ Wieferich primes up to $x$ predicts that there are infinitely
many, see `infinite_isWieferichPrime`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem isWieferichPrime_iff :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ p, IsWieferichPrime p ↔ p = 1093 ∨ p = 3511 := by
  sorry

/--
For any given integer $a > 0$, are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that
$a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$? The case $a = 1$ is trivial, since every prime qualifies
(`isWieferichPrimeBase_one_iff`). So is the case $a = 0$ under our definition
(`isWieferichPrimeBase_zero_iff`), which is why the source's restriction to $a > 0$ is dropped.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_isWieferichPrimeBase :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ a : ℕ, {p : ℕ | IsWieferichPrimeBase a p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Are there any Wieferich primes to base $47$? None is currently known. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem exists_isWieferichPrimeBase_47 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ p, IsWieferichPrimeBase 47 p := by
  sorry

/-- The prime $1093$ is a Wieferich prime: $2^{1092} \equiv 1 \pmod{1093^2}$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isWieferichPrime_1093 : IsWieferichPrime 1093 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- The prime $3511$ is a Wieferich prime: $2^{3510} \equiv 1 \pmod{3511^2}$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isWieferichPrime_3511 : IsWieferichPrime 3511 :=
  ⟨by norm_num, by decide +kernel⟩

/-- The prime $2$ is not a Wieferich prime, so no hypothesis excluding it is needed. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isWieferichPrime_two : ¬ IsWieferichPrime 2 := by
  decide

end WieferichPrime

findings.description: The module docstring cites "P. Ribenboim, *Die Welt der Primzahlen*, 2nd ed., Springer (2006), pp. 242–243." The 2nd edition was published in 2011, not 2006. It is Springer-Lehrbuch, ISBN 978-3-642-18078-1, DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-18079-8, and it is the book whose pp. 242–243 Wikipedia's list links to; these pages fall in chapter 5, pp. 233–261, "Welche besonderen Arten von Primzahlen wurden untersucht?". The 2006 book is the 1st edition (ISBN 3-540-34283-4). The slip comes from Wikipedia's own citation, which gives date=2006 and edition=2nd together with the 2011 DOI and ISBN. The mathematics is not affected.

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement quantifies over every a : ℕ, including a = 0. It uses the ℕ-divisibility p^2 ∣ a^(p-1) - 1 with truncated subtraction, so every prime counts as a "Wieferich prime to base 0". The source (Wikipedia's list, citing Ribenboim) asks: "For any given integer a > 0, are there infinitely many primes p such that a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p^2)?"
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a ≥ 1 we have a^(p-1) ≥ 1, so the subtraction is exact. `isWieferichPrimeBase_iff_pow_modEq` then turns the predicate into p.Prime ∧ a^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2]. Integers a > 0 are exactly the casts of naturals a ≥ 1, and `Int.natCast_modEq_iff` carries the congruence over to ℤ. For a = 0 the Lean set is the set of all primes (`isWieferichPrimeBase_zero_iff`), which is infinite, so the extra a = 0 case always holds. I proved in Lean: (∀ a : ℕ, {p | IsWieferichPrimeBase a p}.Infinite) ↔ (∀ a : ℤ, 0 < a → {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ a^(p-1) ≡ 1 [ZMOD (p:ℤ)^2]}.Infinite), and the ℕ version with 0 < a. The equivalence also holds if Ribenboim's original wording is a > 1 or a ≥ 2, since a = 1 is trivially true as well (`isWieferichPrimeBase_one_iff`). The polarity matches the source's question.

reformulations.difference: The right-hand side is the exact characterization ∀ p, IsWieferichPrime p ↔ p = 1093 ∨ p = 3511. The module docstring phrases the open question as existence: "not known whether there is any Wieferich prime besides 1093 and 3511". Wikipedia's article only records that 1093 and 3511 are the only known ones and that a third must exceed 2^64.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: 1093 and 3511 are Wieferich primes; the file proves this in `isWieferichPrime_1093` and `isWieferichPrime_3511`. So the right-hand side is equivalent to ¬∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 2^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2] ∧ p ≠ 1093 ∧ p ≠ 3511, which I proved in Lean. The theorem's own docstring ("Are 1093 and 3511 the only Wieferich primes?") has the same polarity as the right-hand side. Against the module docstring's existence phrasing the open answer(sorry) slot simply inverts, which changes nothing mathematically.

review.notes:
What I checked, declaration by declaration:

(1) Definition. `IsWieferichPrimeBase a p` means p.Prime ∧ p^2 ∣ a^(p-1) - 1 in ℕ. For a ≠ 0 the subtraction is exact and this is the source's congruence (`isWieferichPrimeBase_iff_pow_modEq`, proved in ForMathlib). For a = 0 every prime qualifies. That value is reachable only in `infinite_isWieferichPrimeBase`, where it is harmless (equivalence proved, see reformulations). For p = 2: 2 is not a Wieferich prime (2^1 - 1 = 1) and not base-47 (46 ≢ 0 mod 4). It is correctly a base-5 Wieferich prime, as in Wikipedia's table.

(2) Parsing. `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ p, IsWieferichPrime p ↔ p = 1093 ∨ p = 3511` parses as True ↔ (∀ p, (W p ↔ (p = 1093 ∨ p = 3511))), confirmed with pp.parens. `answer(sorry)` at Prop elaborating to `True` is the repository default.

(3) Equivalences proved in a scratch file with 0 errors:
- `infinite_isWieferichPrime` ↔ {p | p.Prime ∧ 2^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2]}.Infinite.
- `exists_isWieferichPrimeBase_47` RHS ↔ ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 47^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2].
- The base-a and 1093/3511 equivalences listed under reformulations.

(4) Sanity checks. A fast modular-exponentiation search reproduces [1093, 3511] for base 2 below 10^6, [11, 1006003] for base 3 below 2·10^6, and none for base 47 below 10^6. The Lean predicate agrees with the congruence for all a < 60 (a ≠ 0) and p < 400.

(5) Polarity and status. All `answer(sorry)` right-hand sides have the source's polarity. All four `research open` tags match current sources:
- the list still records all three questions as unsolved;
- a third Wieferich prime must exceed 2^64;
- Fischer's 2025/2026 tables list no base-47 prime (searched to 2·10^14);
- OEIS A039951's first unknown index is 47.

(6) Ribenboim. I could not access the text of pp. 242–243 (Google Books and archive.org give no preview). The verdict does not depend on it: the Lean statement is equivalent whether Ribenboim restricts to a > 0, a > 1 or a ≥ 2.

The only finding is the citation-year slip (2nd edition dated 2006 instead of 2011), copied from Wikipedia's reference.
